https://www.ynetnews.com/article/rjglaqc.text: New footage released Saturday evening shows Mali and Liel Yahalomi alongside the Israeli police officer who located them in Buenos Aires after nearly a week of searches. The two women are seen with Walter Kogan, Israel Police’s representative in South America, during a brief questioning outside the bus on which they were found. Mali is seen smoking a cigarette while Liel and Kogan stand beside her. Police spokesman Aryeh Doron told Channel 12 that Kogan said the two were highly emotional when he met them. “They hugged him, and what really moved them was when he told them, ‘An entire country is worried about you, even outside the bus,’” Doron said. He described Kogan as “a man with a significant intelligence background, a professional who did an excellent job.” After a week in which investigators examined multiple scenarios surrounding the pair’s disappearance, police now believe financial distress was likely a central factor and that the close bond between mother and daughter played a major role in their decision to leave together. “From the beginning, it was clear this was their initiative,” a police source said earlier Saturday. Investigators also uncovered a message sent by Liel to her mother before the trip in which she wrote: “I’ll go with you anywhere.” At an early stage, police examined whether Mali’s work at a bank could be connected to the disappearance. “When we were told the mother worked at a bank, the suspicion immediately arose of a scenario like Eti Alon,” the source said, referring to the former Israeli bank employee convicted in a major embezzlement case. Police contacted the bank and ruled out any theft of funds. Investigators did, however, discover that before the trip Mali withdrew about 14,000 euros in cash from her own money. “When someone leaves with a sum like that, the understanding is that the intention probably isn’t to come back after four days,” the source said. Police are also examining information suggesting money may have been taken from the grandmother and are looking into how much she knew about the plan. Investigators identified several additional actions they viewed as signs of advance preparation, including deleting apps and information from phones and using photos taken in Vienna in a way police suspect was designed to create the impression the women were still there after they had already moved on. Police also noted that Vienna offered access to a major transportation hub, allowing the pair to continue by rail or other means to multiple European countries. Investigators found that Mali made one attempt to call the Israeli consulate in Vienna, but the call went unanswered. Police said it remains unclear why she tried to contact the consulate. Bought phones in Czechia, photographed in Vienna, flew to Argentina The journey did not begin in Vienna, as initially believed, but in Czechia, where phones can be purchased without presenting a passport. Police believe the mother and daughter then continued to Vienna, where they recorded videos intended for their family. Those videos were only sent after the pair had already moved on to another country, believed to be Germany. According to a senior police official, investigators believe the delay was intended to create the false impression that they were still in Vienna. Their phone was last located near a train station in the Austrian capital. From Germany, the two flew to Argentina, where they were found by Kogan. Police believe Buenos Aires may not have been their final destination and that the pair intended to continue elsewhere in South America. Authorities have not disclosed the destination, and it remains unclear whether they ultimately continued their journey. Kogan was dispatched from Mexico to Argentina once investigators established that the pair had reached South America. Police officials said that within hours they obtained information indicating that Mali and Liel had landed in Buenos Aires and boarded a bus heading toward another destination. The concern was that if they continued into a country where law-enforcement cooperation was more limited, locating them would become significantly more difficult. Behind the search was a large Israel Police intelligence operation involving around 300 investigators and intelligence personnel working around the clock to reconstruct the pair’s route.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cddv.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Russia has promised a 'harsh and painful' response to the expulsions By Paul Kirby ,Â Europe digital editor Â and Â Nick Thorpe ,Â in Budapest Published 6 hours ago Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita OrbÃ¡n says 10 Russian diplomats have been ordered to leave Budapest for taking part in "unacceptable" activities. "This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," she wrote on social media, without giving details. Hungary was viewed as Russia's closest ally in the European Union under Viktor OrbÃ¡n for years, but since his election defeat in April the new government has pivoted away from his pro-Kremlin stance. The Hungarian foreign minister said the decision to expel the diplomats "does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia", but the foreign ministry spokeswoman in Moscow said "the response to the Russophobic lobby will be harsh and painful". Hungarian Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar promised "pragmatic" relations with Moscow from the moment his Tisza party was elected in April. He and the foreign minister have both called on Russia to bring an end to the war in Ukraine. In May Anita OrbÃ¡n summoned the Russian ambassador to protest against a big drone attack on the Transcarpathia region of Ukraine that is home to a large Hungarian minority. Commentators have pointed out that her predecessor had not summoned the ambassador since the start of the Russian full-scale invasion in 2022. Then last month Magyar formally broke with the previous Fidesz government's policies, with new guidelines spelling out that Russia's conduct in Ukraine "poses a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order, and also puts the Hungarian minority living in Transcarpathia in serious danger". Russia's Ambassador to Budapest, Evgeny Stanislavov, reacted bitterly to Anita OrbÃ¡n's intention to continue "the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules". Hungary's next PM would pick up if Putin calls and tell him to stop Ukraine war Published 13 April Budapest's promise of pragmatic co-operation was worth absolutely nothing, he complained, adding that Hungary's "extremely unfriendly step constitutes an unprecedented and ungrounded escalation". Before Magyar was voted into office, Hungary had for years insisted on maintaining close relations with Moscow, partly citing cheap Russian oil imports. Viktor OrbÃ¡n objected to the EU's supply of aid to Ukraine and repeatedly delayed packages of sanctions on Russia. Ahead of the April elections, independent Russian investigative website Agentsvo reported that 15 of the 47 Russian embassy staff in Budapest were linked to Russian intelligence agencies and six more might be linked. Former Hungarian foreign intelligence deputy head AndrÃ¡s Telkes told the BBC that even though "Russian spying activity" had been investigated before the election, the Fidesz government had prevented any action being taken. The Russian embassy in Budapest had also rejected as false a report alleging that three Russian military intelligence officers had travelled to Budapest to influence the Hungarian vote. Russia has routinely denied its embassies are used for espionage. However, hundreds of Russian diplomats have been expelled across Europe since 2022, and Russia has responded in kind. Telkes told the BBC that the big question now was how Moscow would respond: "If 10 Hungarian diplomats were to be expelled from Moscow, in a tit-for-tat move, that would effectively close the Hungarian embassy there." Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Reuters Andrew Tate Andrew and Tristan Tate denied US bail as brothers fight extradition to UK Brothers, arrested in Miami in July on UK rape and sex trafficking charges, to remain in custody in Florida Anna Betts Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.46 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A US judge denied the bail request of the controversial social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate on Wednesday, ordering the brothers to remain behind bars as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom. The Tate brothers, prominent figures in the so-called “manosphere”, were arrested in Miami on 18 July after British prosecutors filed new charges against them and sought their extradition to the UK. Those charges included criminal charges of rape and sex trafficking. British prosecutors previously charged the brothers with rape, human trafficking and sexual assault. The Tates, who are dual British-US citizens, have repeatedly denied the accusations against them. The brothers have been held at the federal detention center in Miami since their arrest while they contest their extradition. In a 30-page order issued on Wednesday, US magistrate judge Lauren Louis wrote that the brothers “failed to meet their burden to demonstrate that they do not present a risk of flight or danger to the community, or that special circumstances warrant their release”. “Respondents have failed to demonstrate that special circumstances here warrant relief, whether their proposed special circumstances are considered singly or together,” Louis said. Louis also said the brothers “possess an exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction”. A lawyer for the brothers, Joesph McBride, criticized the ruling. “Detention first. Evidence later, maybe,” he wrote in a statement on X. “Andrew and Tristan Tate have been in federal detention since July 18 on a foreign accusation the United Kingdom has not yet been required to support with a single piece of evidence.” “Every burden in that courtroom falls on Andrew and Tristan,” he continued. “None of it falls on the government that wants Andrew and Tristan handed over. Two American citizens, on American soil, ordered to prove a negative against a case that does not yet exist on paper.” “September 16 is coming,” he said. “God bless.” Per court documents, the UK government has until 16 September to provide information supporting its extradition request and the allegations against the brothers. https://www.hngn.com/articles/273339/202.text: The European Union agreed Tuesday to remove Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its Russia sanctions list and to renew restrictions on about 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years, ending a two-week standoff that had pushed the bloc's sanctions regime to the brink of lapse. Ambassadors sealed the compromise ahead of a midnight Sept. 22 deadline, already extended from Sept. 15, and it was formally approved later that day by written procedure. The asset freezes and travel bans on both men are lifted.EU sanctions require unanimity, which gave individual governments leverage. Latvia, the last holdout, abstained, which allowed the decision to pass. Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said late Monday that he could not accept the proposal and that Europe's pressure must grow stronger as long as Russia continues the war. On Tuesday he described the choice as one between a bad solution and a much worse one.The push began with France, which asked earlier this month for Usmanov to be removed on national security grounds and declined to give details. A senior diplomat in Brussels said Paris explained the request was linked to a potential prisoner release involving French nationals held in Azerbaijan. Other diplomats said Uzbek and French authorities reached an arrangement under which Azerbaijan would release two French nationals in return for the delisting, with a pardon from President Ilham Aliyev; Uzbekistan, where Usmanov was born, reportedly helped facilitate it. France has not confirmed the arrangement, and an Azerbaijani diplomat said Baku wants Usmanov delisted but denied trying to influence decision-making. On Wednesday, Aliyev pardoned French national Martin Ryan, according to reports. Ryan, the head of a Baku-based food-import company, had been serving a 10-year sentence after an espionage conviction in March. Baku accused him of working for France's foreign intelligence service, an allegation Paris rejects.Luxembourg then insisted that Fridman be treated the same way. Fridman, a Russian-Israeli businessman, has filed a multibillion-dollar claim against Luxembourg over his frozen assets, reported as about $16 billion, or 15 billion euros. Slovakia, which had also demanded Usmanov's removal for different reasons, vetoed Fridman's continued listing, diplomats said. In 2024, the EU's General Court annulled earlier decisions listing Fridman for insufficient evidence covering February 2022 to March 2023, but he remained listed because the Council had already issued updated decisions.Usmanov, 73, is a Russian-Uzbek metals and telecoms tycoon who founded the investment company USM Holdings and has an estimated net worth of about $16.6 billion. The EU sanctioned him in March 2022, describing him as having particularly close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and he denies the allegations. The removals apply only to the EU list and do not change sanctions imposed by other countries.Ukraine reacted sharply. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the delisting "shameful and unjustifiable," said Moscow is celebrating, and urged EU governments to impose national restrictions on the two men. President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote that no name on the list is there by accident and that each represents a reason the war started and continues. He had earlier thanked Latvia for its opposition and called for a rollover of individual sanctions without political delistings. The Kremlin said it backed removing the two men and that the bloc should lift sanctions on all Russian businessmen.Latvia moved to impose national sanctions of its own on the two men. Kulbergs also said France had agreed to open talks with Latvia on joining a French nuclear deterrence initiative, a sign of what the country sought in return for stepping aside.The bargain rests on time as much as names. By locking in the other listings for 36 months rather than the usual six, the compromise removes the recurring deadline at which any single member state can threaten a lapse. Hungary's recent change of government has taken away a frequent obstacle to renewals, but this episode showed that leverage can come from other capitals: France on Usmanov, Luxembourg and Slovakia on Fridman. Several EU diplomats said removing people for political reasons sets a dangerous precedent, and one said the episode signals that a delisting can be won through pressure. It was not the first such removal in renewal talks: in March 2025, three others, including Usmanov's sister, Gulbahor Ismailova, were dropped. The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the bloc needed stability by settling the future of the regime.Three things remain open. Whether Azerbaijan releases the second French national has not been reported. Whether other member states follow Latvia with national sanctions on the two men will show how far the delisting is contained. And Luxembourg's litigation with Fridman may now proceed without the listing that froze his assets. Whether a sanctions list built on evidence of ties to the Kremlin can also serve as a bargaining chip is the question the next unanimity vote will test, though under the new schedule that vote is not due for three years.
